en: My blood is not like his;
You will go before your God.
If you make him your kinsman,
He will rush headlong into action,
Your affairs will flare up and collapse.
Until he grows fat he will fawn,
Then rage and prance;
One day he will turn against you,
And blood will stream from your neck.
Your kindness will become his strength,
And bring disaster on your head!
His temper will sour and he will bare his teeth,
He will turn on you in wrath,
His fury will exceed all bounds;
When this wretch reaches full rage,
He will seize you by the throat.
He will study your bearing,
Then, inflamed, provoke your anger;
He will confront you openly,
And your misery will drive you mad.
He will take your people from you,
And cast your affairs into ruin.
He will smash your mouth,
And knock your teeth clean out.
He will make sport of your people,
And bend your back time after time.
He will not heed a word you say,
But strike your eyes from their sockets;
If opposed, he will bind your giant,
And seize your mares as spoil.
If you begin to wheedle him, saying,
“My own blood brother has become lord,”
He will punch your brains out.
Thus he will truly destroy
Whatever wits you have.
When that madman surges forth,
Will he not bring hell upon your host?
Will he not take revenge without stopping?
Will he not overturn my mountain
And raise a riotous uproar?
Will he not rain down volleys of arrows?
Will he not seize and occupy the White Palace?
He will break the strength you girded,
And utterly crush your people.
If you are a lion, if you are a tiger,
If you are truly my wedded lord,
Hear my words, my khan:
In the end Külchoro will gouge out your eyes!
Hero Seytek will pursue you;
If Kanykey and Aichürök still live,
They will bring your sickness to a head.
If your upstart mounts the golden throne,
Bakai will split your crown.
Tell the warriors—tell your men!
Tell the executioner who, when the khan commands,
Takes human noses and ears
And wears them as amulets;
Who drinks and is never sated with blood,
Who grapples and never spares a life,
Who drinks poison when told to drink water,
And scoops blood when told to scoop souls;
Bull-necked and camel-thighed,
Who wrings the life from those he grapples—
Tell that savage wrestler and headsman,
Tell him who stands beneath the banner!
Tell him who, when word comes from the khan,
Levels his spear without delay;
Tell the marksman who never misses,
Who destroys whoever attacks
And delivers punishment with his own hand.
Give the order in your wrath;
Upon the head of the maddened slave
Bring utter and final destruction!
When the wrestlers close in,
Let his head fly off with a crack;
From this vagrant rebel
Let life depart with a shriek.
Let them fit their spearheads,
And begin the combat in full;
Destroy this monstrous villain
And grind him beneath the earth!
You bluster without cause,
Bull-chested and rash-tempered—
Can a hero be like you?
You are no man but mere earth;
Your courage is great, but you have no sense,
You are utterly lacking in wisdom.
Yesterday the crescent-shaped golden banner rose,
And tumult split the sky;
The honored fled and khans died,
And all who fought were slain;
The earth thundered and the people roared
When the fierce battle raged.
He will grimace, thirsting for blood,
While turmoil closes over his head;
“What can a lifelong comrade do?”—
As his soul departs, Kanchoro
Will plead, “Oh, my comrade!”
Your noble blood will turn to ash,
Your good fortune turn to night,
Your throne be filled with tormenting demons,
And grief become a day of calamity.
Firing his gun and drawing his bow,
He will take away your arrows,
Drive back your host,
And mount and seize your throne.
He will cut down and shatter your fortune,
Bring spectacle and chaos to your camp,
And openly launch rebellion.
Roar out your command
And take the sword in hand!
That crooked, vile traitor—
Finish him utterly!
Understand all the words I have spoken;
Cut off this slave’s head
And from the top of a post
Hang it dangling!
Let your troops close in from every side,
Let Külchoro’s head be struck off,
Let the orphan Seytek be subdued,
And let the women, children, and remaining herds
Be scattered once again!
He clings to you as kin,
While enemy blood is spilled;
Let the crooked one’s schemes collapse,
And let no ill-willed, inwardly treacherous
And openly hostile enemy
Stand against this accursed palace of yours.
Tell the sentries, tell the guards
To seize and slaughter this slave.
Tell the good men who raise you high,
Tell the shaman who strikes the lungs,
Tell your wrestlers and your lions,
Those who wreak slaughter through the ages,
Who throw not merely women, but noble men,
And even the khagan into panic.
His valor was extraordinary—
Let us tell of that valor:
His bristling moustache
Was like the saber of a Bukharan,
And the breath from his mouth
Like flame from a smithy’s furnace.
Crackling like lightning,
Like a keen black falcon,
He flashed with fury;
His heart grew cold, his innards burned,
And a dreadful conflict began.
That noble soul, once roused, could not be restrained;
Such was the mighty eagle
Whom they bound by a single hair.
“If you call me a slave, a slave I am,
Yet I am the watching black eye
Of my late gray-wolf brother!
I broke through Jet-Kait and opened a road.
I spread strife across the earth,
Hardened by drinking blood,
And won fame as a leopard-warrior.
I knew that I would die,
Yet, pampered woman, my disgrace,
I have burned with devotion to you.
In the splendid palace you were mistress,
While I was an orphan, countless as grains of sand.
You cared for me in my orphanhood;
Though you did not give me milk from your breast,
You gave me doe’s milk.
You filled my life with delightful words;
While my dear brother lived,
You became like a mother to me.
Over your countless horses, withheld when asked,
I shall cast the cold lasso;
The golden throne withheld despite entreaty,
I shall seize without entreating.
It was not darkness—become night itself!
When bloodthirsty Kyyaz was slaughtered,
You alone mourned and veiled yourself.
You who befriended Kyyaz,
Your wrath boiled and arose;
You were a hero versed in many things.
You began this desperate revolt and great turmoil,
Seeking to save your life;
Why then did you leave alive
This warrior doomed to die in madness?
He has begun strife among your multitude;
Unless you kill him and take revenge,
In the end he will destroy you!
Seize your wrestlers and lions firmly
And put him down,” she said;
“Bind the maddened slave!”
The pampered woman Chachykey
Rose raging from the palace,
Haranguing Kanchoro,
Shouting for the wrestlers
And summoning her Kanchoro.
The pampered, vicious shrew
Stirred boundless conflict,
Pressing Kanchoro hard,
So eager was she for strife.
Before the wrestler-guards could swarm,
Before the wrestlers could close in,
Before the queen could give her order,
Before the people could assemble,
The wearer of eighty-four pieces of armor,
Who flared when roused like crimson fire,
Whose courage was stern and venom strong,
A scourge born among mortals—
Külchoro, upheld by the spirit Shay,
Braced himself like a leopard.
Inspiration came to him from the unseen;
His bloodlust seized him fiercely,
He ground his teeth with a crack,
Gripped by valor, his fury boiling;
His thirst for blood possessed him.
When this gray wolf blazed with rage,
She gave you tea when you thirsted,
Listened freely to your words,
Cosseted you,
Hung necklaces around your neck,
Draped brocade over your back,
And, lest the sun’s heat touch you,
Had you tended in a shady place,
Entrusted you to attendants,
And had the chief wife praise you.
Did she not regard you as a nephew
And graciously listen to your words?
She listened to your fitting words as a daughter-in-law,
And regarded you as her own mother.
Yet you let your tongue run wild,
Incited your Kanchoro,
And destroyed your bloodthirsty lord.
You steeped your churn in poison,
And thus brought about your own end!
You placed sixty treasuries of jewelers
In Kanchoro’s hands;
You made Kanchoro destroy
The sixty Kalmyks, Bölökbay,
And Davut, master of the treasury.
You imposed punishment upon me
And had strips of hide cut from my back;
Into the palace where no cold-hearted man might enter,
You admitted Kanchoro.
You shook the Kyrgyz and made them your subjects,
And made heroes of whomever you chose.
Woman, if you understand, it was you
Who caused this monstrous revolt and great conflict.
You are an infuriated infidel,
An evil, witch-like infidel!
You utterly ended my laughter,
And scattered all my possessions;
You made my words mere meadow grass
And devastated my people.
Incorrigible shrew, you will never prosper;
Though you came here a wanderer, you bluster
And will not curb your pride.
May you and your husband be as one!
How you have enraged me,
And driven my spirit into grief;
